checks.rationale: All 36 opening argument segments are identified as Anderson, including the explicit outline-only qualification and the inference from necessary thoughts to a mind. Jump begins his paraphrase only at the closing edge of the clip; no part of that reply is credited as Anderson's reason.

Jump gives the full descriptive account, examples of alternative logics, and correspondence-based conclusion. Anderson contributes a brief acknowledgment and begins his follow-up at the clip's closing margin, not the substantive argument selected for Jump.

Anderson distinguishes truth bearers from truth makers and develops the two written sky statements sharing one truth. Jump's opening overlap and brief agreement are separately identified; the exact quotation and inferential reasoning belong to Anderson.

Jump explains propositions as a subset of statements, cites the formal-language description, and denies a further entity beyond correspondence. Anderson briefly repeats the subset claim as a question and resumes his objection at the end; neither intervention supplies Jump's selected reasoning.

Anderson supplies the English/French sky example, shared propositional-content claim and inference about communication. Jump's unicorn response starts only after Anderson explicitly finishes his argument; the selected quotation remains Anderson's own wording.

Jump develops the translated unicorn description and the analogy from invented fiction to propositions. Anderson supplies only a brief acknowledgment inside the passage and a clarifying question afterward; the comparison and conclusion are consistently Jump's.

Anderson alone gives the modal example of a physically empty possible world still making a claim true, then concludes that truth differs from its physical expression. Jump's disagreement begins in the following margin after that conclusion.

Jump distinguishes the empty world's facts from truth as a property of the describing sentence and explicitly denies truth prior to expression. Anderson's acknowledgment and resumed objection occur after the completed distinction; no contrary speaker's premise is attributed to Jump.

Anderson develops the natural-number infinity argument and the discovery analogy, then draws the distinction between truths and finite human expressions. Jump's qualified agreement starts after that conclusion; the selected quotation about more truths than statements belongs to Anderson.

Jump supplies the finite-alphabet example yielding infinitely many potential statements. Anderson's preceding question and following challenge are separately identified; the audio confirms Jump's crucial word potentially and does not convert potential combinations into actual human utterances.

Anderson contrasts the accessible physical ocean with an abstract statement and challenges the combination of abstract entities with physicalism. Jump introduces the preceding emergence comparison and resumes with brain emergence only after Anderson's objection is complete.

Jump identifies abstract things as emergent brain properties and develops the shrink-ray illustration followed by labeled neurological patterns. Anderson briefly repeats the emergence claim as a question; Jump explicitly confirms it and supplies the account, so the attribution is unchanged.

Anderson distinguishes alterable Sherlock Holmes fiction from logical and mathematical truths and concludes that the latter do not depend on our thinking or speaking. Jump's Star Wars comparison appears at the clip margins; the contrast and exact quotation are Anderson's.

Jump explicitly compares mathematical descriptions with Star Wars descriptions and says their truth depends on correspondence to reality. Anderson's objection about fictional correspondence follows the selected comparison; the conclusion and counterfactual belong to Jump.

Anderson develops the rain versus arithmetic contrast, explains necessary truth as truth in every possible world, and infers that contingent human expressions cannot be the necessary truths. Jump's initial language comment and following disagreement are not credited to Anderson.

Jump acknowledges necessary and contingent facts, assigns necessity to reality, and distinguishes a necessary fact from its contingent description. The quoted descriptive-thing formulation is clearly Jump's; Anderson returns to truth bearers afterward.

Jump explicitly proposes replacing statements with ideas understood as biochemical interactions and describes truth through their correspondence to reality. Anderson's denial that ideas are physical begins only after Jump completes this account; attribution requires no source alteration.

Anderson asks about true ideas and develops the two-ideas/one-truth distinction through the shared sky claim, concluding with abstract propositions. Jump's initial yes and following key-maker analogy are separately identified and do not supply Anderson's inference.

Jump gives the independently made keys opening the same lock and explicitly denies a necessary third category. Anderson introduces the universals objection only after the completed analogy; Jump's exact quotation remains within his uninterrupted explanation.

Anderson explains why two keys sharing a shape raises the same question about universals, and explicitly says the illustration does not settle that issue. Jump's brief acknowledgment does not contribute a premise; the sustained counterargument is identified as Anderson throughout.

Anderson distinguishes unicorns from ideas about unicorns and asks whether propositions are nonexistent objects of ideas or are themselves ideas. Jump's comparison precedes the rebuttal and his renewed question follows it; the exact quote and critical distinction belong to Anderson.

Jump distinguishes things in heads from things in the world, groups propositions with imagined language items, and denies their independent existence. Anderson's category question precedes the selected explanation and his Socrates question follows it; the central account is consistently Jump's.

Anderson gives the abstract-versus-physical category challenge and asks for the status of the shared Socrates proposition. Audio restores a missing ASR negation in the conditional English-language illustration: then there is no such thing, not an affirmative existence claim. The frozen selection rationale already identifies the consistency challenge; its meaning, attribution and selected quotation are unchanged, and the raw caption is preserved.

Jump responds with the two written Socrates sentences sharing the English-language label and presents the label as imagined rather than another independent entity. Anderson's short question precedes the explanation and his follow-up follows it; the quoted labeling claim is Jump's.

Jump contrasts a socially constructed definition of truth with the independent reality that ideas may describe. Anderson begins the truthmaker objection only at the transition after Jump's distinction; the selected description and exact quotation remain correctly assigned to Jump.

Anderson explicitly accepts correspondence while redirecting the question to what things bear truth and identifying propositions as those bearers. Jump's agreement and later social-construction response are separately labeled; Anderson supplies the selected question and explanation.

Anderson develops the objection that imaginary truths would leave knowledge without a real object, using their shared knowledge of two plus two equals four. Jump's request for repetition and tentative response are separately labeled at the boundaries; the sustained objection and selected quotation belong to Anderson.

Jump explains how constructed statements and truth labels can correspond to an independently existing truthmaker, then asks where the contradiction arises. Anderson's preceding fragment and subsequent equivocation objection are outside the central response; the constructive explanation is consistently identified as Jump's.

Anderson asks whose individual idea could constitute the singular shared Socrates proposition and distinguishes a private mental instance from the proposed shared bearer. Jump's opening clarification and closing return to keys are separately labeled, leaving the selected challenge correctly attributed to Anderson.

Jump returns to multiple working keys and argues that descriptive propositions can be dispensed with because reality exists independently. Anderson begins restating that position at relative second 36.396, after Jump's completed claim at 34.746; this confirms the transition already recorded in the inventory and preserves the selected quotation's attribution to Jump.
